title: Welcome
excerpt: Welcome to Chulapa. This is another Jekyll themethat you can use for creating your site.
content: Welcome to Chulapa. This is another Jekyll theme that you can use for creating your site.   Motivation   In the last couple of years I created some tiny websites using GitHub Pages. However, I was not very happy with some of the thousands of Jekyll themes available, since I didn’t find one that met all my requirements:      Easy to use   Awesome looking   Plenty of add-ons   Feed   So, as a way to challenge myself, I decided to build this one from scratch. My main references were Beautiful Jekyll and Minimal Mistakes, that are two pretty good options, much more mature than this one and with hundreds of users. So, why not learn from them? There are pieces and components of these themes on this one.   One theme, a thousand looks   Without prior knowledge of CSS, I taught myself about rules, specificities, flexboxes, etc. through implementing Bootstrap v4 as the CSS base of Chulapa.   This is not the first theme with this implementation, but I found the way to configure it via _config.yml, which allows any user to easily change the look of the site without needing to write CSS or SCSS. On top of that, implementing Bootstrap themes from third parties is fast and reliable.   The huge advantage is that, if you give it a go, you can use Chulapa in any site you want but still define a unique look to each of them. No one could notice that the theme is the same!   Next steps   When this post was written in May 2020, Chulapa was still in development. Stable releases are now available; see the installation guide for setup instructions.   The theme currently uses Bootstrap 4 and Font Awesome 6, with support for Font Awesome 5 and optional v4 shims. See the changelog for subsequent changes.

title: Ask Chulapa
subtitle: A new way to explore the documentation
excerpt: Ask questions about Chulapa and get practical examples with links to the docs.
content: The Chulapa documentation now has an AI assistant. You can open it from the sparkle button on the homepage or documentation pages and ask about installation, skins, configuration, layouts and other documented features.   Try a specific question such as “How do I change my site’s skin?” or “How do I add a local video?” The assistant can provide short explanations, code examples and links to the relevant documentation. Each question is independent, so include the details it needs rather than relying on an earlier message.   Recent messages and the draft stay in the current tab’s sessionStorage so reloading a page can restore the interface. Clear chat resets those messages and the draft. This displayed history is not sent as conversation context: each request contains only the current question.   Following a link from the assistant in the same tab closes its panel so you can read the destination. Reopening it restores your messages and draft. Opening a link in a new tab leaves the original panel open.   The assistant uses Cloudflare Workers AI with a reviewed summary of the docs. Questions are sent to Cloudflare for processing. Answers can contain mistakes; check the linked documentation, especially before changing your configuration. Site search remains available when you want to explore the original pages.   This is an addition to the documentation site. It is not bundled with the reusable theme and does not require an AI account to use Chulapa on your own site.   I wrote a more personal account of the development, including context selection, answer testing and the mobile interface, on my blog: Building a documentation chatbot for Chulapa.

title: Chulapa v2.1.0: more control over your site
subtitle: New looks, more search options and better metadata
excerpt: Explore Chulapa v2.1.0, from page metadata and new skins to search and layout options, with a small preview of what comes next.
content: Chulapa v2.1.0 is here. This release gives you more control over how your site looks, how readers find its content and how pages appear when shared. When I first built Chulapa, I wanted a theme I could use for different sites while giving each one its own look. The idea is still the same. You can choose a skin, change a few settings in _config.yml and make the site your own. This release adds more ways to do that, along with some useful fixes behind the scenes. Here are the changes I would start exploring. Give each page the right introduction A page title has several jobs. It introduces the content on the page, appears in the browser tab and helps describe a link when someone shares it. You may want different wording for each of those places. In v2.1.0, seo_title and og_title let you set the metadata titles separately from the visible heading. The new description option also gives you an explicit metadata description, independent of the subtitle and excerpt: --- layout: default title: "My field notes" subtitle: "A weekend exploring the mountains" seo_title: "Mountain field notes | My travel blog" og_title: "A weekend in the mountains" description: "Routes, observations and practical notes from a mountain weekend." --- The theme shares that description across HTML, Open Graph, Twitter/X cards and JSON-LD, without forcing it into a fixed character limit. You can keep the introduction on the page conversational and write a separate description for people encountering its link elsewhere. There is more control over the rest of the metadata, too. canonical_url provides a consistent preferred URL across the page’s metadata, breadcrumbs and feeds. Page language and Open Graph locales can be configured separately, and translated locales can be listed. Article metadata includes publication and modification dates, authors, sections and tags where supplied. For sites with several contributors, the JSON-LD publisher can now be configured independently of the author. Sharing images can have explicit alternative text, dimensions and a MIME type, while schema_image identifies representative article images for structured data. These settings help describe your content accurately. They do not guarantee a particular search result or social preview, so check a few real pages after updating. The metadata reference and global settings explain the options and their defaults. One theme, more looks This release adds 13 skins, including listen, navi, cyborg, darkly, slate, solar and the butterfly variants. There are also more code highlighting styles, including github.dark, nord, one.dark and stackoverflow.light. The configuration stays familiar. For example, to combine the Navi skin with Nord code highlighting: chulapa-skin: skin: navi highlight: nord Browse the skin previews and syntax highlighting examples to compare them with your own content. Skin names are case-sensitive: use the filename without its .scss extension. Titles and subtitles now support Markdown as well as HTML. A little emphasis or an inline code name can be written using the same syntax as the rest of your post. Give readers another way to find your content Chulapa now supports Fuse.js...

Publishing the documentation   A push to main starts this repository’s GitHub Pages workflow. It installs Ruby dependencies from docs/Gemfile, builds the documentation with Jekyll, uploads the generated site and deploys it to Pages. The workflow can also run on its schedule or be started manually.   flowchart TD   accTitle: Publishing the Chulapa documentation   accDescr: A push to main, a scheduled run or a manual trigger starts GitHub Actions. title: Publish your first site with Chulapa
subtitle: See your own blog online using only your browser
excerpt: Create a blog from the template, change its title and edit a sample article, then open your published website.
content: By the end of this tutorial, you will open a public blog with your own site title and an edited article. Use the supplied example throughout; you can choose colors and add photographs after publishing. Start with the GitHub template Sign in to a free GitHub account and use your browser, preferably on a computer. No software installation is needed. The Chulapa 101 example shows the blog you will personalize. Your copy will be public. Do not add passwords, private photographs or other information you do not want to share. 1. Create your site Open the template. In Repository name, enter my-blog, choose Public and create the repository. A repository is the folder containing your site’s files on GitHub. Check: the repository belongs to your account and shows a list of files. 2. Enable publishing In your new repository, open Settings > Pages. Under Build and deployment, select GitHub Actions as the source. The template already includes the files needed to publish; you do not need to add a workflow. Check: Pages shows GitHub Actions as its publishing source. 3. Name your blog Return to Code, open _config.yml and click the pencil button. This is the file for your site settings. Find these existing entries and replace their values. For a GitHub account called ana and a repository called my-blog: title: "My first blog" repository: ana/my-blog url: "https://ana.github.io" Use your own account and repository names. Replace the existing entries; do not paste another copy or replace the whole file. Keep the other settings and spaces, including baseurl: the template sets the site’s path for you. Click Commit changes. This saves a version of the file. Save to your repository’s default branch (main or master in the template); publishing starts automatically. You can edit the article while it runs. Next, open index.html in Code and click the pencil. Change only its existing title line, between the opening --- lines, to: title: "My first blog" Keep the filename index.html and all other content. Save with Commit changes on the same branch. This changes the heading visitors see on your home page. Check: both saved files contain “My first blog” as their title. 4. Write your first post In Code, open _posts/, choose a sample article and click the pencil button. Keep its filename and the settings between the two --- lines. Change only its title entry to: title: "Hello, this is my website" Replace the article text below the second --- line with: Today I am publishing my first story. Click Commit changes and save to the same default branch. Check: the saved article contains your title and sentence. 5. Open your published website Open Actions and find the publishing run for your latest saved change. Wait for it to finish successfully. Publishing may take a few minutes. Open the website address shown in Settings > Pages. Check the site title, then open your edited article. If you are viewing files on github.com, return to Pages and open the website address instead....

title: Theming Chulapa
subtitle: Appearance settings reference
excerpt: This page lists appearance settings. For a task, use Choose a skin,Change a color, Change fonts orChange code highlighting. For relationships betweensettings, read How skins and overrides interact.For custom Sass and the Codeply sandbox, use Adapt a Sass skin.
content: This page lists appearance settings. For a task, use Choose a skin, Change a color, Change fonts or Change code highlighting. For relationships between settings, read How skins and overrides interact. For custom Sass and the Codeply sandbox, use Adapt a Sass skin.   Settings belong in _config.yml and compile into CSS during the build. Local preview needs a Jekyll restart after configuration changes.   Skins                  Field       Values / default       Constraint                       chulapa-skin.skin       Exact skin filename without .scss; default none. Examples: journal, gitdev, lux, flatly.       Names are case-sensitive on case-sensitive filesystems; unknown names fail the Sass import.                 skin: none       No predefined skin assignments.       Bootstrap/theme defaults and explicit vars still apply.                 skin: auto       Loads the generated palette as the selected skin.       Independent of the optional later autothemer step.           The skin catalog provides the named previews. Its current-site preview is not a skin named current. Procedure: Choose a skin.   Load Google Fonts                  Field       Value / effect                       googlefonts       List of mappings with a url for each font stylesheet; no additional fonts when absent.                 chulapa-skin.vars.font-family-base       Body font-family expression, including fallback families.                 chulapa-skin.vars.headings-font-family       Heading font-family expression.           Loading a stylesheet does not apply its families. Other font providers use the existing custom-head hook. Procedure: Change fonts.   Code highlighting   chulapa-skin.highlight selects a highlighting stylesheet; its default is default. The setting selects appearance, while Rouge performs syntax highlighting. Style specimens show the available styles. Procedure: Change code highlighting.   Autothemer   chulapa-skin.autothemer enables the palette-generation step after skin and vars when set to the YAML boolean true; omit it or use false to disable that step. It is independent of skin: auto. Its default primary color is Bootstrap 4’s #007bff when not already assigned.   Existing skin and vars assignments remain in effect. Procedure: Enable Autothemer. Rationale: How skins and overrides interact.   Variables   chulapa-skin.vars is a mapping of supported Bootstrap/theme Sass variable names to Sass expressions. Names omit the leading $ and trailing ;. Hex colors, font lists and sizes are quoted strings; switches such as enable-rounded are YAML booleans. For example:   chulapa-skin:   vars:     body-bg: "#000"     body-color: "#eee"     font-family-base: "Montserrat"   The corresponding Sass assignments are $body-bg: #000;, $body-color: #eee; and $font-family-base: Montserrat;. A font stylesheet is a separate input; the fonts guide includes a complete loading/application example.   The variable dictionary lists common inputs; Bootstrap’s variable source contains the full Bootstrap definitions. See also the Bootstrap 4 theming reference. Calculated helpers such as landingpage-card-bg and cactus-btn-text are not overridable through vars. Custom CSS handles rules without exposed variables; see custom HTML and styles.

title: Layouts and snippets
subtitle: Layout, snippet and page-option reference
excerpt: Look up layouts, snippets and page settings, with links to content-editing guides.
content: Use this page to look up a layout, snippet or page setting. For everyday editing, use Create a post, Create a page or Add an image. A layout is a page design; front matter is the settings block between --- lines at the top of a content file. Moving existing posts or pages? Use the migration front matter mapping. Choose a layout or an optional feature The default layout works for ordinary articles and pages. Use Minimal for a simpler page or Landing page for a prominent introduction. The reference below covers page options, indexes, galleries and custom layouts; you do not need to configure them all. Features marked v2.1.1-dev are available on main, but are not included in v2.1.0. An unpinned remote theme follows main; a pinned release or installed gem only provides the features included in that version. Recent feature How to enable it Availability Mermaid diagrams Page front matter: mermaid: true, plus Mermaid code blocks v2.1.1-dev PhotoSwipe galleries Liquid include parameter: photoswipe=true v2.1.1-dev Active TOC section Automatic with an in-page, sidebar or kramdown TOC and JavaScript v2.1.1-dev GoatCounter analytics Site setting: goatcounter, plus a production build v2.1.1-dev A. Layouts General purpose Default Use default for articles and ordinary pages. Add this to the settings block at the top of the file: --- layout: default --- You can avoid typing this on each page by setting this layout as the default layout for all the pages via _config.yml and front matter defaults: defaults: - scope: path: "" values: layout: "default" Options Additional options you can set on the front matter or via defaults: Jekyll also accepts these settings in the same front matter block: Setting Use layout Choose a layout from this guide. permalink Set a page’s address, such as /contact/. published Set false to omit a page or post from the normal build; this does not protect private files. slug Set the slug used by a post’s address pattern. categories, tags Group articles and provide the labels used by badges and related cards. excerpt_separator Override the site’s post excerpt boundary. sitemap Set false to exclude the page from jekyll-sitemap. locale Override the site language for this page. Component switches such as show_date, show_author, show_toc, show_comments and show_breadcrumb are off when unset, unless your site’s defaults enables them. show_header is a separate opt-in for minimal; see Optional header. title, subtitle: Visible heading and subtitle for supported header types; also used when generating metadata. date, last_modified_at: Date of the page and last modification date. See here to learn the accepted format of dates. excerpt: Brief description of the content. If not provided Chulapa would create it as the first paragraph of the content. Note that in the case of documents under posts Jekyll allows additional options. description: Explicit metadata description, independent of the visible subtitle and excerpt. See SEO metadata for precedence. mathjax: Set to true to load MathJax for mathematical notation. mermaid: Set to true to render Mermaid diagrams. title: Accessibility and performance
subtitle: Check your site's navigation, colors and resources
excerpt: Verify your published pages with a keyboard, narrow screens and real content.
content: Use this guide to check a published site after changing content, a skin or an integration. Have the home page, a representative article and search open, along with any galleries, videos or comments you use. Some expected controls require main after v2.1.0, not the v2.1.0 gem or pin. Compare your installed version with the behavior reference. These checks do not establish WCAG compliance by themselves. Check your own pages Open those pages at a narrow phone width and enlarge their text. Confirm that content remains readable and controls stay reachable. Check long headings and your actual images, not only short sample content. Repeat after fixing a problem. Use the steps below for each representative page. Record the page, browser, viewport and problem so you can verify the same case after changing it. Keyboard navigation Use Tab without a mouse. Confirm you can see which link or control has focus. Activate Skip to content when available and check that it bypasses the menu. Open and close your menu and dropdowns. Use Enter for links, Enter/Space for buttons and Escape where a panel supports it. Confirm focus returns to the trigger after closing the floating menu. If you use the sidebar TOC, open it, Tab through its controls and close it with Escape. Check that closed controls are no longer reachable and that section highlighting does not move keyboard focus while you read. In a PhotoSwipe gallery, open an image, browse with arrow keys and close with Escape. Check the return to the image link. Try search, comments and your other widgets too. For exact supported behaviors and fallback limits, use the keyboard reference. If you use custom layouts or widgets, check their headings, labels and controls as well as the theme’s own navigation. Colors and content Check text and link contrast on the actual backgrounds after changing colors. Confirm that links remain distinguishable without relying only on color and that keyboard focus is visible. Use meaningful link text, such as “View my portfolio”, rather than “Click here”. Review informative photographs for descriptive alternative text. Gallery snippets supply generic descriptions; use custom image markup where the individual photograph conveys information. Give videos a descriptive name and provide captions/transcripts where needed. Give Mermaid diagrams accTitle and accDescr and explain complex diagrams in prose. Begin article sections with ## below the page title. Enable reduced motion in your device/browser settings and reload an automatically cycling carousel. Check that it starts paused, that play/pause is operable and that the chosen state survives interaction as described by the motion reference. PWA and offline behavior Do not infer offline support from a favicon, manifest or an app-like window. The theme provides no built-in offline mode; see offline constraints. If you added a separate offline implementation, disconnect the network and test the published pages and integrations before promising that behavior to visitors. title: Migrating from another Jekyll theme
subtitle: Keep your content and URLs while switching themes
excerpt: Move an existing Jekyll site to Chulapa with a pinned remote theme and a practical migration checklist.
content: Keep your posts, pages and images. This guide assumes your site already builds with Jekyll and has a _config.yml and Gemfile. Before switching themes: save a backup or create a migration branch. Theme-specific settings and layouts are not converted automatically; check the preview before publishing. Follow steps 1–5, then use the migration checklist. For field-by-field lookup, use the separate migration mappings. 1. Prepare your site Create a migration branch or backup. Record your home page, a post, a page, search and feed URLs so you can check them after switching themes. Keep your existing url, baseurl, permalink and custom domain settings unless you intend to change your public addresses. Check local overrides first. Files in _layouts, _includes and assets with the same paths as theme files take precedence. Old copies can hide the new design or keep loading old scripts. Review them individually; move obsolete theme copies outside the site source, preserving your own content and customizations. Keep useful custom layouts and includes, then adapt their parent layouts, include paths and CSS to the new theme. For site-wide additions, prefer the supported custom hooks reference over copying a complete theme layout. 2. Switch to a pinned remote theme In _config.yml, remove the old theme and replace any existing remote_theme: remote_theme: dieghernan/chulapa@v2.1.0 Add these entries to your existing plugins list, keeping unrelated plugins: plugins: - jekyll-remote-theme - jekyll-include-cache In your Gemfile, add these dependencies if missing: gem "jekyll-remote-theme" gem "jekyll-include-cache" Remove the old theme gem if nothing else uses it. Keep Jekyll and dependencies needed by your content or publishing workflow. The personal-blog Gemfile provides a dependency reference; merge it with your file rather than replacing it. Run bundle install. Pinning @v2.1.0 keeps the migration on a released version. Omitting the tag follows development updates. Features documented as v2.1.1-dev, including Mermaid, PhotoSwipe and GoatCounter, are not in v2.1.0. 3. Adapt layouts and front matter Review _config.yml defaults as well as the settings between --- lines in posts and pages. Explicit page values override defaults: an old layout: post will still need changing even if you set a new post default. Use the layout and front matter mappings to identify the fields your old theme used. Check the relevant entries rather than renaming every setting indiscriminately; conversions are not automatic. Keep standard fields such as title, date, categories, tags and intended permalink values. Check old theme-specific includes and CSS classes in the content; translate or replace them using the layout and snippet reference. See live demos to choose a suitable layout. For example, replace the old layout and header settings in an existing post’s front matter with these values, preserving its title, date and other content: layout: default header_type: post show_date: true include_on_feed: true 4. Reconnect navigation and integrations Rebuild navbar and footer links manually: links from your previous theme are not imported automatically. Re-enter them in navbar.nav and footer.links, then open every destination in the preview. Edit existing sections in _config.yml; settings from the previous theme are not translated automatically.
